title: Integrating QPUs into Supercomputing Centers Using Slurm HRES Plugins | NVIDIA Technical Blog
gist: Slurm 26.11 adds Hierarchical Resources (HRES) Lua plugins that let supercomputing centers schedule QPUs as native cluster-level resources tied to reachable nodes, fixing the idle-node, multi-QPU and upgrade-fragility problems of GRES and license/SPANK workarounds. Open source QRMI and QDMI plugins already exist, with IBM, IQM, Pasqal, Quantinuum, Alice & Bob and MQSC integrating, supporting NVIDIA's thesis that every supercomputer becomes hybrid quantum-classical.

insights.claim: NVIDIA's quantum team argues every supercomputer will eventually become a hybrid quantum-classical system, with national programs in North America, Europe and Asia already installing QPUs alongside HPC systems.
insights.speaker: Stefano Mensa
insights.so_what: Hybrid quantum-GPU supercomputing is a demand vector for NVIDIA's HPC/accelerated-computing stack beyond pure AI; watch national-lab QPU procurements.
insights.quote: Every supercomputer will eventually be a hybrid quantum-classical device

insights.claim: The first power users of quantum-GPU supercomputing are expected to be existing HPC scientists in chemistry, weather modeling and engineering simulation, who will treat the QPU as just another accelerator next to CPUs and GPUs.
insights.speaker: Stefano Mensa
insights.so_what: Quantum adoption likely flows through existing HPC user bases and centers, favoring vendors embedded in HPC software stacks.
insights.quote: For these scientists, the QPU is simply another accelerator

insights.claim: Until Slurm 26.11, the lack of a workload manager able to natively schedule QPUs was a key missing piece blocking researchers from adopting quantum processors into workflows.
insights.speaker: Stefano Mensa
insights.so_what: Removing the scheduler bottleneck lowers integration friction for QPU deployments at supercomputing centers.
insights.quote: Until now, a key missing piece has been a workload manager.

insights.claim: Because schedulers had no native way to model a QPU, quantum integrations at supercomputing centers have been custom-built per site and per QPU builder, so users face different interfaces, admins maintain upgrade-blocking custom code, QPU vendors rebuild integrations per customer, and global systems integrators cannot deliver repeatable deployments.
insights.speaker: Stefano Mensa
insights.so_what: A standard scheduler interface could compress QPU deployment cost/time and favor vendors that ship portable plugins.
insights.locator: Until now, schedulers have had no native way

insights.claim: Modeling a QPU as a Slurm generic resource (GRES, the GPU mechanism) binds it to a single compute node, so only jobs on that node can use it and a node failure leaves the QPU unreachable until an administrator reconfigures the cluster.
insights.speaker: Stefano Mensa
insights.so_what: Explains why QPUs are cluster-wide accelerators architecturally distinct from GPUs in HPC scheduling.
insights.quote: A QPU is typically a cluster-wide accelerator, not part of a node.

insights.claim: The common workaround of Slurm licenses plus SPANK plugins can leave compute nodes idle while jobs wait for the QPU, allows device options without a license, struggles with multiple QPUs on one cluster, risks breakage on every Slurm upgrade, and cannot detect when a QPU is recalibrating or offline.
insights.speaker: Stefano Mensa
insights.so_what: Idle-node waste and upgrade fragility were real operating costs for early quantum-HPC sites; HRES targets these directly.

insights.claim: Slurm 26.11 introduces Hierarchical Resources (HRES) plugins that schedule a QPU as a native cluster-level resource associated with the specific set of nodes allowed to use it; HRES first appeared as a beta in Slurm 25.05 as an evolution of licenses.
insights.speaker: Stefano Mensa
insights.so_what: Marks the point at which quantum hardware becomes a first-class scheduled resource in the dominant HPC workload manager.
insights.locator: Modeling a QPU as a hierarchical resource

insights.claim: HRES splits responsibilities so site-specific details and policies (endpoints, reachable nodes) live in an admin-controlled resources.yaml while device logic lives in a Lua plugin that a QPU vendor or community can write once and ship to every Slurm 26.11 site.
insights.speaker: Stefano Mensa
insights.so_what: Write-once portability turns QPU integration from bespoke services work into reusable software, lowering vendor go-to-market cost.
insights.locator: A site describes the QPU as a cluster-level HRES

insights.claim: Slurm treats a QPU as a single schedulable unit and does not orchestrate calibration, error correction or device control, which stay in the QPU's own runtime behind third-party access middleware, so the approach applies both to today's NISQ devices and future error-corrected systems.
insights.speaker: Stefano Mensa
insights.so_what: The architecture is hardware-agnostic and future-proof, reducing technology-bet risk for centers buying QPUs now.
insights.locator: Slurm treats the QPU as a single schedulable unit.

insights.claim: HRES Lua plugins do not link against libslurm, so vendors can ship and update them independently of Slurm's release cycle without rebuilding on every upgrade, and each resource gets its own plugin context so one cluster can host multiple QPUs and QPU types.
insights.speaker: Stefano Mensa
insights.so_what: Multi-vendor QPU hosting on one cluster becomes practical, supporting a multi-provider market rather than single-vendor lock-in.

insights.claim: HRES plugins admit or hold a job before its nodes are allocated, so jobs never hold idle compute nodes while waiting for the QPU, and an ESLURM_HRES_REMOTE_FAIL code keeps jobs pending without draining nodes when the external quantum service is unavailable.
insights.speaker: Stefano Mensa
insights.so_what: Improves utilization of expensive classical nodes in hybrid workflows, a concrete efficiency gain for supercomputing centers.
insights.quote: so the job never holds idle nodes while it waits for the QPU

insights.claim: Open source QPU middleware communities QRMI and QDMI have already released HRES plugins on Slurm 26.11 APIs: QRMI books QPU access per job with the user's credentials, while QDMI only admits jobs and leaves queueing to the provider.
insights.speaker: Stefano Mensa
insights.so_what: Two distinct integration models (reserve vs. provider-queue) are already available, accelerating center adoption.
insights.locator: Community integration examples of HRES plugins

insights.claim: Quantum ecosystem organizations integrating HRES plugins include Alice & Bob, IBM, IQM, MQSC, Pasqal and Quantinuum, letting Slurm 26.11 sites connect to quantum computers from multiple providers.
insights.speaker: Stefano Mensa
insights.so_what: Broad vendor participation signals Slurm HRES becoming the de facto quantum-HPC integration standard; watch IBM, IQM, Pasqal and Quantinuum HPC-center deals.
insights.locator: Learn how more organizations in the quantum ecosystem
